newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: Ex-military ruler favorite in Bolivia election.
newsitem.headline: Ex-military ruler favorite in Bolivia election.

text.p: Bolivians went to the polls on Sunday to elect a new president in a vote widely expected to be won by Hugo Banzer, a right-wing general who in 1971 seized power in a coup and ruled with an iron fist for seven years.
But no candidate was likely to garner a strong-enough majority in Sunday's vote, which was progressing in calm.
"I hope this very low level of violence lasts for a long time in our democracy," outgoing President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada said at the National Electoral College.

If opinion polls prove right Banzer, of the right-wing Nationalist Democratic Alliance (ADN) will face ex-President Jaime Paz Zamora of the Revolutionary Left Movement (MIR) in a runoff in Congress next August.
The 71-year-old general does not deny charges that in his drive to stamp out Marxist guerrillas from land-locked Bolivia, one of Latin America's poorest nations, human rights were badly abused.
"Only in that era?" he said when asked about cases of disappearance, torture and forced exile under his regime.

"I took control of a country that was living in anarchy and chaos," he told Reuters late on Saturday. "Violence was not one sided. It was inevitable. You couldn't just go out there with a little white handkerchief and a flower. No way."

After being ousted himself in a coup in 1978 (one of nearly 200 in Bolivia's history), he decided to embrace democracy, formed the Nationalist Democratic Alliance (ADN), and ran five times for president, once winning the popular vote but being defeated in the congressional runoff.

Paz Zamora, a democratic president between 1989-1993 who trails Banzer by around 10 percentage points in opinion polls, has problems of his own -- the White House last year cancelled his entry visa due to his alleged links with drug-trafficking.

Paz Zamora denies the charges, but outgoing President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada, a staunch U.S. ally, has made a point of insisting that if Paz Zamora were to become the new leader Bolivia would be shunned by the community of nations.

The ruling party candidate, Juan Carlos Duran, has an honest but also an uncharismatic image -- an unforgivable sin in a country that has always favoured Latin "caudillos" -- and is trailing in a distant third place.

Aside from tarnishing Paz Zamora's image, drugs were hardly a campaign issue in this Andean nation, which along with Peru and Colombia produces virtually all the world's coca leaf and cocaine, most of which finds its way to the inner-city streets of the United States.

Coca is part of everyday life for millions of native Bolivians who honour the ancient tradition of chewing its leaves or drinking them in tea and who see the cocaine problem as just a "gringo" aberration.

All top candidates have espoused the country's 12-year-old free-market and privatisation drive, which has consistently elicited praise of the international financial community but which appears to be testing the limits of Bolivians' patience.

Sensing the discontent with railways, telephones and services whose post-privatisation rates have shot up beyond the reach of many Bolivians, most of whom live under the poverty line, Banzer has promised to "humanize" the economy.
Besides the president and vice-president, whose term will now be five years instead of four, Bolivians will also choose all 27 senators and 130 deputies.
